title: Information bottleneck · relevance
question: What is preserved by T = A when X = (A, B) is two independent fair bits and Y = A?
choices: Two input bits and zero label bits
One input bit and one label bit
Zero input bits and one label bit
One input bit and zero label bits
explanation: Knowing A leaves B unknown but predicts Y exactly. Thus I(X;T) = I(T;Y) = 1 bit.

title: Information bottleneck · objective
question: What objective trains the classifier in this paper?
choices: An explicit IB loss at every layer
A KL penalty against the theoretical IB encoder
explanation: IB supplies a theoretical comparison; the reported network uses cross-entropy training without additional explicit regularization.

title: Information bottleneck · dpi
question: Why can a layer gain label information during training without violating data processing?
choices: Data processing never applies to neural networks
Labels are always injected at inference
Later layers manufacture new label information
explanation: DPI compares successive representations for a fixed Markov chain. Across training checkpoints the weights, and therefore that chain, change.

title: Information bottleneck · bins
question: Four distinct activations enter two bins. What can a fall in measured input information mean?
choices: All exact activations must be identical
Quantization merged states even though exact values differ
explanation: A deterministic injective map on four equally likely inputs retains two exact bits; the two equally occupied bins retain only one.

title: Information bottleneck · beta
question: What does increasing beta in I(X;T) − beta I(T;Y) emphasize?
choices: Increasing the number of training bins
explanation: Beta weights the reward for relevant information. At beta zero, forgetting everything minimizes the objective.

title: Information bottleneck · encoder
question: What mismatch appears in the IB encoder assignment?
choices: KL divergence between input and group label distributions
explanation: The encoder favors groups with similar label distributions through exp(−beta KL), also weighted by group mass.

title: Information bottleneck · diffusion
question: What characterizes the reported late diffusion regime?
explanation: Small mean gradients relative to batch fluctuations motivate a diffusion approximation; weights keep evolving and useful compression is not guaranteed.

title: Information bottleneck · evidence
question: What can we conclude from the 400 versus 10,000 epoch descriptions?
choices: One layer and six layers have identical compute per epoch
Depth reduced reported training epochs in that synthetic experiment
explanation: The paper describes different attainment milestones and architectures, without matched numerical stopping criteria or wall-clock measurements.

title: PAC-Bayes · nonvacuous
question: What makes an error bound nonvacuous?
choices: It is smaller than training error
explanation: Error is always at most 1. A bound below 1 adds information, although a binary-task bound above 0.5 need not certify an improvement over fair guessing.

title: PAC-Bayes · classifier
question: Which predictor is directly covered by this paper’s PAC-Bayes certificate?
choices: The classifier averaged over draws from Q
explanation: The bounded quantity is population classification error averaged over weight draws. A guarantee for a mean network or vote needs additional reasoning.

title: PAC-Bayes · variance
question: In v = w + √s ⊙ ξ, what does s contain?
choices: Variances of individual weights and biases
A covariance shared between all pairs of weights
explanation: The posterior covariance is diag(s). Sampling uses √s because standard deviation, not variance, multiplies a standard-normal draw.

title: PAC-Bayes · prior
question: Why is the prior centered at the original random initialization?
choices: It was fitted to the test labels
It is equal to the final posterior mean
It makes all KL costs zero
It is independent of the training sample and preserves an initial parameter reference
explanation: The fixed-prior theorem permits this data-independent center. Centering freely at trained weights after observing data would not be justified by that theorem.

title: PAC-Bayes · selection
question: How does the paper justify choosing the prior variance using training data?
choices: A union bound over a predeclared countable grid
Ignoring the selection because variance is a scalar
Replacing the prior mean with the posterior mean
Using the raw test error as a bound
explanation: The candidate variances receive confidence budgets proportional to 1/j². Their total failure probability is bounded by delta; continuous optimization is followed by grid evaluation.

title: PAC-Bayes · optimization
question: What changes during PAC-Bayes bound optimization?
choices: The original prior center and test labels
The posterior mean, posterior variances and relaxed prior variance
Only the last sampled network, with no distribution retained
explanation: The posterior mean can move from the SGD solution. Fresh noise estimates loss gradients while the original initialization stays fixed as the prior center.

title: PAC-Bayes · confidence
question: Why are there two inverse-KL steps in final certification?
choices: To correct Monte Carlo error, then bound population error from training data
To train the mean network twice
To certify both the mean network and a majority vote
explanation: Finite posterior sampling and finite training data produce different uncertainties. With delta = 0.025 and delta prime = 0.01 the combined confidence is at least 0.965.

title: PAC-Bayes · evidence
question: What does the random-label table value 1.352 represent?
choices: The bound for the T-600 mean network
A square-root complexity diagnostic indicating vacuity
explanation: Section 4.4 specially reports √(BRE/2) for random labels. It is not an inverse-KL probability, which must lie in [0,1].

title: Bayesian SGD · mass
question: What distinguishes Bayesian evidence from the best training fit?
choices: Evidence integrates likelihood under the prior
Evidence is the maximum likelihood alone
explanation: A narrow high peak can contribute less integrated mass than a broader region. The prior measure is part of the comparison.

title: Bayesian SGD · coordinates
question: What must accompany a change of parameter coordinates for exact evidence to remain invariant?
choices: Keep the old numerical prior regardless
Transform the prior density with its Jacobian
Keep only the largest Hessian eigenvalue
explanation: A coordinate change preserves the model only when its probability measure is transformed consistently. General nonlinear changes can still affect a Laplace approximation.

title: Bayesian SGD · sign
question: If the source defines Z / Znull = exp(−E), what does E = −2 mean?
choices: The null is favored by exp(2)
The learned model is favored by exp(2), before prior model odds
explanation: The minus sign means negative E favors the learned model. Evidence odds are not error rates.

title: Bayesian SGD · sampler
question: Why is ordinary SGD not established here as an exact posterior sampler?
choices: Its noise is generally anisotropic and parameter dependent
explanation: The exact Langevin argument uses appropriately scaled isotropic noise and limiting assumptions; the analogy to SGD is not an exact sampling theorem.

title: Bayesian SGD · fullbatch
question: What does the no-momentum formula g = ε(N/B − 1) give at B = N?
explanation: A full batch contains all examples, so batch-selection noise disappears. The approximation εN/B is unsuitable at this endpoint.

title: Bayesian SGD · scale
question: In the small-batch momentum approximation, what compensates for increasing m from 0.9 to 0.95?
choices: Double B at fixed ε and N
explanation: The denominator 1−m halves. Doubling B preserves εN/[B(1−m)] approximately, within the model’s regime.

title: Bayesian SGD · optimum
question: What does the batch-size experiment imply at fixed learning rate?
choices: An interior optimum can balance useful noise and fitting
explanation: The tested setup has an interior optimum; batches around ten or smaller fail to train. This is not a universal numerical optimum.

title: Bayesian SGD · metrics
question: Why can stable test accuracy coexist with rising test cross-entropy?
choices: The test labels must have changed
Wrong predictions can become more confident without changing their class
explanation: Accuracy depends on the predicted class, while cross-entropy penalizes the probability assigned to the true label. Confidence can deteriorate without changing accuracy.

title: Double descent · procedure
question: What can change effective model complexity while parameter count stays fixed?
explanation: EMC belongs to the full training procedure and labeled-data distribution; training longer can alter fitting ability.

title: Double descent · threshold
question: Where does the proposed critical regime lie?
choices: Always at one parameter per sample
Where EMC is comparable to the number of training samples
explanation: The fitting boundary depends on the procedure and data, so raw parameter count is not a universal locator.

title: Double descent · noise
question: How are noisy image labels assigned in these experiments?
choices: Sampled once, then kept across augmentations
explanation: A corrupted label is fixed for that image; it is drawn uniformly from the incorrect classes.

title: Double descent · loss
question: A predictor assigns probability 0.25 to its observed class. What is its cross-entropy?
explanation: Cross-entropy is −log(0.25), not the binary correct/incorrect indicator used for classification error.

title: Double descent · time
question: Why can a fixed-width model show epoch-wise double descent?
choices: Its fitting ability changes as training proceeds
New layers are added every epoch
explanation: The weights and optimization state evolve while the architecture stays fixed, potentially carrying the procedure through the critical regime.

title: Double descent · samples
question: How can adding data hurt the specified learner locally?
choices: It always lowers the quality of every label
It can move an overparameterized procedure toward the fitting threshold
It necessarily increases its parameter count
explanation: Increasing sample size can move the fitting boundary; its shift can temporarily outweigh the benefit of more data at a fixed width and procedure.

title: Double descent · stopping
question: What does the updated paper say about optimal early stopping?
choices: It always removes every form of double descent
It often removes effects, but Figure 19 is a model-wise exception
It always makes more data harmful
explanation: The authors report a CIFAR-100 exception and do not observe more-data harm with optimal early stopping; neither statement is a universal theorem.

title: Double descent · hypothesis
question: What is the status of the generalized EMC claim?
choices: A proof for every neural network
An informal hypothesis supported by experiments
explanation: The tolerance and width of the critical regime are not generally derived, and the paper does not prove a universal scaling law.

title: Grokking · transfer
question: What makes a held-out pair reuse a fitted training answer exactly?
choices: Its embedding sum equals the training pair’s embedding sum
explanation: Identical inputs to the same fixed decoder produce identical outputs. The training input must already have the correct target.

title: Grokking · injective
question: Why does Proposition 2 assume an injective decoder?
choices: To guarantee that every optimizer converges
To infer equal decoder inputs from equal fitted targets
To guarantee zero classification loss at finite logits
explanation: Equal outputs can come from different inputs for a noninjective decoder. Injectivity supplies the reverse implication under the zero-loss idealization.

title: Grokking · objective
question: Which loss trains the actual toy predictor?
choices: Task MSE or cross-entropy through the decoder
explanation: The effective embedding loss is a surrogate for analysis. Actual task gradients update both the embedding table and decoder.

title: Grokking · rank
question: What does nullity two imply for ordinary-addition constraints?
choices: There are exactly two training examples
The decoder must have two layers
All held-out target classes were seen
Every embedding coordinate is affine in the symbol index
explanation: The constant and index vectors span the nullspace when no extra degrees of freedom remain. This describes geometry, not decoder coverage of targets.

title: Grokking · rate
question: In the linear relaxation, what happens if the positive slow rate λ3 halves at fixed η?
explanation: The paper’s qualitative spectral timescale is 1/(ηλ3). It is not an exact accuracy threshold for Adam and a neural decoder.

title: Grokking · phases
question: Why can more decoder weight decay fail to improve generalization?
choices: It always removes the training split
Excessive restriction can cause confusion and prevent fitting
It changes ordinary addition into modular addition
explanation: The reported phase diagrams include confusion as well as comprehension, grokking and memorization. Useful settings depend on the competition between both modules.

title: Grokking · censoring
question: What do Figure 4’s runs that miss RQI > 0.95 by 10,000 steps establish?
choices: They did not reach that representation threshold within the budget
Their held-out accuracy is exactly zero
explanation: These are censored observations of a representation metric. They do not prove infinite delay or give an exact held-out accuracy.

title: Grokking · pca
question: What does a circle in two PCA coordinates prove about the transformer?
choices: Every other variance component is zero
The affine ordinary-addition theorem applies unchanged
It reveals visible structure, but not that the full effective dimension is two
explanation: The PCA projection is evidence of structure. The entropy-based effective dimension uses the full variance distribution and need not equal the number of displayed axes.

title: Binarized networks · objective
question: What trains the BNN in this study?
choices: A weighted sum of BDM and entropy
explanation: BDM and entropy observe weight snapshots; neither is an explicit training penalty.

title: Binarized networks · ste
question: Why use a straight-through estimator?
choices: To supply surrogate gradients through discrete operations
To replace all hidden layers with entropy
explanation: A literal sign derivative is zero away from its discontinuity. The exact surrogate is not specified in the supplied main text.

title: Binarized networks · baseline
question: What distribution does the entropy baseline summarize?
choices: Output logits on the test set
explanation: Both metrics use the same block decomposition, so entropy already sees local pattern frequencies.

title: Binarized networks · cost
question: A tile with toy CTM cost 5 occurs four times. What is its BDM contribution?
explanation: The distinct tile cost is paid once, plus log₂4 = 2. These are teaching costs, not actual lookup values.

title: Binarized networks · zero
question: What does zero block entropy mean?
choices: Only one tile identity is observed
explanation: A single observed block identity has probability one. Its description and repetition can still have nonzero BDM cost.

title: Binarized networks · correlation
question: If loss and complexity both decline together, what correlation can result?
explanation: Positive correlation means they move together. Common time trends can generate association without a causal mechanism.

title: Binarized networks · evidence
question: Which result limits a universal BDM advantage?
choices: Neither UCI HAR variant shows a consistent advantage
explanation: Table 3 has overlapping intervals and lower BDM midpoints on both engineered-feature and raw UCI HAR.

title: Binarized networks · invariance
question: What happens when whole tiles are rearranged without changing their counts?
choices: Both count-based metric summaries stay the same
explanation: Both formulas depend on distinct tile identities and counts, not their positions. The underlying network function can still change.
